beats.narration_text: Hej, Liam. Today: component-showcase — the riff skill. Render a visual unit with a themed educational example. Critique it in the Teardown voice: what it does, where it's useful, pros and cons. Then stop. Liam, in for Bear.

beats.narration_text: Two halves. Render: the harness renders each scene with a fixture — themed educational example content, teardown palette. Riff: author the NBB Teardown script per scene — what it does, pros and cons, educational usefulness — then ElevenLabs voice and captions. Assemble into one compilation reel per functional category.

beats.narration_text: Five phases. Select the target batch or scene. Fixture: supply themed educational example content via the fixture library. Render on the user's Mac — harness renders and logs failures, never drops silently. Riff: write the NBB script per scene. Assemble into a per-category compilation reel. Pilot one lane before scaling to all.

beats.narration_text: Self-demo: fixture plus riff script for SkillTeardownMechanism — free, no harness render, no ElevenLabs. The fixture supplies a real educational example: quantum tunneling, act one. The riff script follows the NBB structure: what it does, pros, cons, educational use. This is the script the human reviews before approving ElevenLabs spend.

beats.narration_text: Law one: riff is the inform arm of bench promotion. It renders and critiques so the human can see each scene and hear its trade-offs. The human decides what to keep or promote. Riff is the evidence base for that decision — not the decision itself. Inform before decide. That's the phase boundary.

mechanismLines: Inform arm: renders evidence + critique; promotion decision is human-only

Every failure logged (slug + reason) — no silent drops

beats.narration_text: Law two: riff never decides what to keep or promote — it surfaces pros and cons and stops. That refusal is the point. Principles four, five, and six. The skill with the power to promote would be a different skill. Riff keeps the human in the promotion decision so the bench evolves under human editorial judgment, not automation.

props.quote: Riff never decides what to keep or promote — it surfaces pros/cons and stops. That refusal is the point (principles 4 + 5 + 6).
mechanismLines: Refusal is a design choice, not a limitation
Bench promotion is irreversible — requires human editorial judgment
Riff asked to promote → declines; lays out pros/cons instead
Human decides; riff generates the decision brief

beats.narration_text: Law three: rendering and ElevenLabs spend happen on the user's machine, after the human verifies the scripts. Riff authors; it does not spend. The script is reviewed before the voice runs. The render is gated behind the pilot lane. No unverified spend. No mass-produced reels before the pilot proves the harness.
